title: Grade 7 Science — Fri, Jun 27
description: Heat — Day 5 of 5: Full mixed review — conduction, convection, radiation
subject: science

questions.question: What is the difference between heat and temperature?
options: They are the same
Heat is total thermal energy (joules); temperature is average kinetic energy of particles (°C or K) — a large cold lake has more heat than a tiny boiling water drop
Temperature is energy; heat is the measurement
Heat is measured in degrees; temperature in joules
questions.explanation: Temperature = average KE per particle. Heat = total thermal energy. A large cold body has more total energy than a tiny hot body. That's why a swimming pool at 20°C has far more heat than a burning match at 800°C.

questions.question: Which mode of heat transfer requires direct contact between particles?
options: Convection
Radiation
Conduction
All three require contact
questions.explanation: Conduction: heat transfers particle-to-particle by collision (direct contact). Particles vibrate more but don't move. Convection: fluid particles move (no rigid contact needed). Radiation: no particles needed at all — waves travel through vacuum.

questions.question: In convection, why does hot liquid or gas rise?
options: Heat makes it heavier
Hot fluid expands → becomes less dense → lighter → rises; cool dense fluid sinks → creates convection current
Hot fluid is attracted to the ceiling
It rises because it is hotter, not because of density
questions.explanation: Convection: hot → expands → lower density → rises. Cool → contracts → higher density → sinks. This creates a circular convection current. This explains sea breezes, room heating (heater at floor level), and boiling of water.

questions.question: A metal spoon placed in hot tea becomes hot quickly. The wooden handle of a pan stays cool. Which mode explains each?
options: Radiation for both
Convection for both
Conduction (spoon = good conductor; wood = poor conductor/insulator)
Spoon = convection, wood = radiation
questions.explanation: Metal spoon: conduction (electrons and vibrating particles transfer heat along metal rapidly). Wood: poor conductor — particles don't transfer energy efficiently. Both are conduction, just very different conductivities. Metals have free electrons that aid heat conduction.

questions.question: Why is a hot water bag placed at the BOTTOM of a tank rather than at the top?
options: Bottom is safer from leaks
Hot water at the bottom heats → rises; cooler water sinks to replace it, setting up convection → entire tank is heated evenly
Heat sinks downward from a heater at the top
Cold water rises and hot water sinks
questions.explanation: Heater at bottom: hot water rises (less dense), cold water sinks (more dense). This sets up convection currents that heat the entire tank uniformly. Heater at top: hot water stays at top (already less dense); no current forms; only the top heats.

questions.question: We feel warm near a fireplace even if the air between us and the fire is cool. Which mode of heat transfer explains this?
options: Conduction through the air
Convection currents bringing warm air
Radiation: infrared waves travel directly from fire to skin without heating the air in between
Both conduction and convection equally
questions.explanation: Radiation: electromagnetic (infrared) waves travel from the fire in all directions and are absorbed directly by our skin. Air is not heated by this process — that's why we feel warm even in cold air near a fire. Conduction through air is negligible; convection rises upward.

questions.question: Wool sweaters keep us warm NOT because they produce heat, but because:
options: Wool generates heat when worn
Wool traps air — air is a poor conductor — the trapped air prevents body heat from escaping by conduction
Wool reflects all radiation back
Wool absorbs sunlight and converts it to heat
questions.explanation: Wool (and fur, down) trap air in their fibres. Trapped air = excellent insulator (poor conductor, no convection). Your body generates heat; wool + trapped air form an insulating layer preventing heat loss. This is conduction prevention, not heat generation.

questions.question: A thermos flask minimises heat transfer in all three modes. Match: (1) Vacuum (2) Silvered walls (3) Glass material — to the mode each blocks.
options: 1=Radiation, 2=Conduction, 3=Convection
1=Conduction+Convection, 2=Radiation, 3=provides structure
1=Convection, 2=Conduction, 3=Radiation
1=Radiation, 2=Convection, 3=Conduction
questions.explanation: Vacuum: no particles → blocks conduction (particle contact) and convection (no fluid flow). Silvered walls: reflects radiation back (shiny = poor absorber/emitter). Glass: poor conductor itself, but mainly provides mechanical structure. Together = near-perfect insulation.

questions.question: In which mode of heat transfer do particles physically move from one place to another?
options: Conduction only
Radiation only
Convection only — fluid particles carry energy as they move; in conduction, particles only vibrate in place; in radiation, no particles move at all
Both conduction and convection
questions.explanation: Key distinction: Conduction = energy transfers but particles stay in place (vibrations pass on). Convection = particles move (bulk fluid flow). Radiation = no particle movement, pure wave energy. Convection cannot occur in solids because particles are fixed.

questions.question: Land breeze blows from land to sea at night. Why?
options: Sea is cooler at night
At night, land cools faster than sea (sea retains heat). Air over warm sea rises; cooler air from land rushes in to fill the gap — this is a convection current (land breeze)
Wind changes direction with the moon
Gravity pulls air toward sea at night
questions.explanation: Night: land cools fast; sea stays warm (high specific heat). Warm sea air rises → low pressure over sea. Cooler land air flows toward sea = land breeze. Day: land heats faster; warm land air rises; sea breeze blows from sea to land. Classic convection driven by temperature differential.

questions.question: Why are cooking utensils made of metals with wooden or bakelite handles?
options: Only aesthetic reasons
Metals conduct heat efficiently to food (good conductors); wood/bakelite are insulators (poor conductors) — handle stays cool and safe to hold
Bakelite is a better conductor than metal
Handles are made of rubber for electrical safety
questions.explanation: Metal body: conducts heat from stove to food quickly. Wood/bakelite handle: poor conductors (insulators) — heat doesn't travel easily from metal body to handle → you can hold it without burning your hand. Thermal conductivity of metals >> wood >> air.

questions.question: Why should a room heater be placed on the floor, not on the ceiling?
options: Electricity regulations
Hot air rises → if heater is on the floor, rising warm air sets up convection currents that heat the entire room; heater on ceiling would heat only the top (hot air stays up)
Heaters look better on the floor
Radiation from floor heaters is stronger
questions.explanation: Convection: hot air rises, cool air sinks. Floor-level heater → hot air rises → circulates whole room. Ceiling heater → already-warm air stays at top; no circulation below. That's why factories use floor heating, and why 'hot air rises, feet are cold' in tall rooms with ceiling heaters.

questions.question: The Sun heats the Earth from 150 million km away. This is possible ONLY because of:
options: Conduction — Earth is connected to Sun by rocks
Convection — hot gas flows from Sun
Radiation — infrared and visible light waves cross the vacuum of space
Gravity transfers energy
questions.explanation: The 150 million km between Sun and Earth is mostly vacuum. Conduction and convection both need matter. Only radiation (electromagnetic waves) can cross a vacuum. Solar radiation heats Earth's surface; Earth re-radiates infrared (trapped by greenhouse gases = global warming).

questions.question: A doctor uses an infrared thermometer (no-touch) to check body temperature. A chimney is made tall to improve draft. A tile floor feels colder than a carpet at the same temperature. Match each to: radiation, convection, conduction.
options: IR thermometer = conduction; chimney = radiation; tile = convection
IR thermometer = radiation; chimney = convection; tile = conduction
IR thermometer = convection; chimney = conduction; tile = radiation
All three use conduction only
questions.explanation: IR thermometer = detects body's infrared radiation (radiation). Chimney height = tall chimney creates stronger convection draft (hot smoke rises, pulls fresh air in at bottom). Tile vs carpet = tile conducts heat from your foot faster than carpet (carpet traps air = insulator) — conduction.

questions.question: A farmer covers plants with polythene at night to protect from frost. On a cloudy night the same protection isn't needed. Which mode of heat transfer explains BOTH facts?
options: Conduction
Convection
Radiation — plants lose heat as infrared radiation to the sky; polythene reflects it back; clouds also reflect/absorb ground radiation and re-emit some back, so ground stays warmer on cloudy nights
Conduction and convection equally
questions.explanation: Both involve radiation: (1) Clear night: plants radiate infrared to cold sky → lose heat → frost risk → polythene reflects IR back. (2) Cloudy night: clouds absorb and re-radiate some IR back to earth → less heat loss → warmer. Polythene mimics what clouds do. Explains frost on clear nights.
